title: Stock Market Today, May 1: S&P 500 and Nasdaq Power to New Highs
content:
Today, May 1, 2026, Apple’s upbeat outlook helped propel tech to fresh Nasdaq records even as the Dow slipped and caution lingered.
The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.29%) rose 0.29% to 7,230.12, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.89%) climbed 0.89% to 25,114.44 on tech strength and fresh records, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI 0.31%) slipped 0.31% to 49,499.27 as value and cyclicals lagged.
Apple gained 3% after beating earnings estimates and offering upbeat guidance, powering mega-cap tech. Five9 soared roughly 30% on strong earnings, reassuring investors concerned about artificial intelligence (AI) disruption of software stocks. Software peers Atlassian and Twilio both surged.
Wolfspeed jumped about 26% after announcing new executive appointments. Cboe Global Markets rallied almost 9% to lead financials.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq extended gains today, breaking new ground as strong tech earnings powered markets despite energy price uncertainty and valuation warnings.
WTI crude spiked above $106 per barrel in intraday trading before finishing at $103. Top energy firms, ExxonMobil and Chevron, warned that oil stockpiles and reserves are running low, and prices could increase dramatically if traffic through the Strait of Hormuz does not resume soon.
In addition to Apple’s strength, memory stocks outperformed with big gains from Sandisk and Micron Technology. Data from Bloomberg shows that over 80% of quarterly earnings for S&P 500 companies have beaten estimates.

title: S&P 500, Nasdaq end at fresh records on tech earnings strength
content:
The Nasdaq and S&P 500 soared to fresh records Friday, cheering mostly strong earnings from tech giants and continuing to shrug off the prolonged US-Iran war that has lifted oil prices.
The records came on the heels of upbeat results from Apple, which rose 3.2 percent, extending the positive sentiment on Wall Street on a day when several leading bourses in Europe and Asia were closed.
"The war is not over but the market doesn't care," said Adam Sarhan of 50 Park Investments.
"That tells me that the reaction to the news is extremely bullish and until we see any heavy selling show up, the bulls are in control."
Analysts have pointed to a winning corporate earnings season as a factor behind soaring markets. Companies in the S&P 500 are on track to report earnings growth of 27.1 percent, the highest rate in more than four years, according to Factset.
"The latest US earnings season has been robust, which has helped prevent global markets from suffering big losses despite the impact of the Iran conflict," said AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould.
Oil prices slid after Iranian state media reported that Iran delivered the text of a new proposal to mediator Pakistan on Thursday evening.
However, US President Donald Trump rejected the proposal.
"At this moment I'm not satisfied with what they're offering," Trump told reporters, laying blame for the stalled talks with Iran due to "tremendous discord" within its leadership.
While oil prices retreated, both major contracts remain above $100 a barrel as the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively shut down.
ExxonMobil Chief Executive Darren Woods warned prices could go higher, noting that the oil market has so far been able to manage the dislocation because of the amount of crude in commercial inventories and the release of some strategic governments reserves.
However, those supplies are running their course, he said.
"So there's more to come if the strait remains closed," Woods said on an earnings conference call with analysts.
Several markets were shut in Europe and Asia for the May 1 holiday, including in France, Germany, Hong Kong and mainland China.
Among markets that were open, Tokyo climbed while London fell, weighed by British bank NatWest, which reported higher quarterly net profit but warned economic conditions were deteriorating.
The European Central Bank and the Bank of England both held interest rates steady on Thursday but signaled possible increases ahead.
The US Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan also kept borrowing costs unchanged this week.

title: Big Tech powers the market with strong earnings wins
content:
Concurrent Wealth Management chief investment strategist Leah Bennett joins Josh Lipton on Market Domination Overtime to discuss what investors should watch as Big Tech navigates geopolitical volatility.
Technology is winning right now. Um, it's interesting. I think we've had this been going on for a little over a year now and if you think about the reasons why technology and I would say the adoption and the efficiencies from technology are really driving the market. Um, we've never gone through a period like COVID where we've really had true supply chain issues as well as labor issues for as long as companies had them and companies had to come up with solutions and not necessarily band-aids, longer term solutions. So we've had this massive adoption not only of AI but of technology in general of robotics and that now we're far enough along where it's really driving the efficiencies. And when you look at companies that are reporting, um, like United Healthcare reported last week, you're having a lot of companies that have been perpetual underperformers and they're starting to get efficiencies from the adoption of technology. So, United Healthcare is an example. Um that stock I think was up 7 or 8% when they reported and their operating margins were supposed to come in at 7.6% and instead they came in at 8.3%. So, um I do think it's why the market continues to go up in the face of these geopolitical and um potential policy um mistakes. That's that's that's basically what the battle is and it'll be interesting to see if that continues, but that is the tailwind.
Leah, you we had a lot of big tech names report this week. I'm just curious more broadly, what do you make of this earnings season, of what you've seen and heard uh of the earnings growth you've seen and what do you think earnings growth looks like ahead?
Yeah, it's a great question. Um, if you look at the S&P 500, um earnings growth was expected to be um 14.1% for the year back in October. Then it was revised up in April up to 18%. Now as of May 1st, earnings are expected to be up over 22%. And it really is because we're starting to see operating margins improve. That's falling to the bottom line. You're seeing earnings increase and you see it with with Apple today. I mean part of the reason that Apple was up, certainly there's expectations around the um the iPhone uh 17 in the super cycle, but you saw revenues come in, um expectations for the next quarter be around 14 to 17% versus um an expectation of 9.1 and their gross margins expanded by 220 basis points. So it really is this efficiency that's driving um the earnings growth and certainly multiple expansion.

title: Why Apple Stock is Jumping on Friday
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.
Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) shares climbed more than 4% on Friday after the company reported quarterly revenue and profit above Wall Street forecasts and gave a stronger sales outlook for the current period.
Apple said fiscal second-quarter revenue reached $111.18 billion, while earnings came in at $2.01 per share. Both figures topped estimates, with Apple supported by solid demand across its flagship products and services.

Apple's iPhone business remained the main driver, with sales up 21.7% from a year earlier to $56.99 billion. Services revenue rose 16.3% to $30.98 billion, while Mac, iPad and wearables also posted gains. Apple said the iPhone 17 lineup continued to draw strong interest.
For the fiscal third quarter, Apple expects revenue growth of 14% to 17% and gross margins of 47.5% to 48.5%. Apple also authorized an extra $100 billion in share repurchases, even as investors continue to watch supply pressures, AI strategy and the planned handoff from Tim Cook to John Ternus.

title: 3 Stocks That Could Be Your Easy Ticket to Creating Generational Wealth
content:
These are all giants in their industries, and they have proved their mettle over time.
There are a variety of reasons people invest in the stock market. Beyond near-term benefits like making money from growth stocks and even long-term benefits like passive retirement income, investing in the stock market can help you create generational wealth.
In general, stocks you can hold forever and pass on to the next generation are going to be solid, established stocks that can withstand the vicissitudes of time. Apple (AAPL +3.26%), Amazon (AMZN +1.25%), and Netflix (NFLX 1.74%) are three great candidates.
Image source: Getty Images.
Apple has created a formidable ecosystem of interconnected devices that sets it far above the competition. Users love the Apple experience and tend to become loyal fans, upgrading to new devices and buying an array of Apple products that all work together. Putting the user experience first, and launching designs, features, and services to achieve that, keeps customers coming back.
The company has been rolling out Apple Intelligence at a pace that has lagged some of its peers, but customers haven't been put off by that, and the iPhone continues to be a hot seller. Management is also planning a major overhaul of Siri, expected in the coming months, that could change the way users interact with their devices and attract even more customers. Plus, the market is now lauding its slower rollout, since it's planning the launch at a fraction of the cost of the other hyperscalers.

Apple has been an incredible wealth generator over time, and it's the kind of company that should continue to be a leader in its space for years.
Amazon recently became the largest company in the world by sales. It continues to generate higher sales and robust profits, and it's the top company in two major growth sectors, e-commerce and cloud computing.
One little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" owns the technology Nvidia, AMD, and Intel cannot function without. And it is still just a fraction of Nvidia’s size.
We just released a brand-new report with the full story and the company’s name.
Although the market has been concerned about its artificial intelligence (AI) spending, the company maintains that it's positioning itself for a huge shift to the cloud. It's planning to spend $200 billion in capital expenditures this year, and management says demand is outsize, and that it's monetizing capabilities as fast as it creates infrastructure.
There is so much going on at Amazon at any specific time, and it's not just AI. The company's Leo satellite program is a real competitor to Elon Musk's Starlink business, and it recently launched the fastest satellite antenna ever built.
Whatever the next trend is in tech, you can bet Amazon will be there, capturing market share and offering gains for long-term shareholders.
Netflix has faced down new competitors in its industry, emerging as the clear winner in streaming. Though the naysayers have predicted its demise several times, it has adapted its model to fit changing trends, and it's that flexibility that makes it such a compelling long-term stock to own.
Today, it offers both premium and ad-supported subscriptions, including syndicated movies and shows, as well as its own content, live sports, games, and more. It has several growth drivers in new subscriptions, increased pricing, and ads, and revenue increased 16% year over year in the 2026 first quarter. It's also become highly profitable, with a 31.5% operating margin in the quarter.
Netflix has become the top name in streaming, and it should continue to reward shareholders for years.

title: Apple Warns the Memory Shortage Is Getting Worse. Experts Say It Could Drive Up Prices
content:
Colin is an Associate Editor focused on tech and financial news. He has more than three years of experience editing, proofreading, and fact-checking content on current financial events and politics. He received his M.A. in journalism from The New School and his B.A. in history and political science from McGill University.
Eric Thayer / Bloomberg via Getty Images
Get personalized, AI-powered answers built on 27+ years of trusted expertise.
A reminder from Apple, just in case Wall Street forgot: There’s a memory shortage.
Apple (AAPL) CEO Tim Cook on Thursday warned headwinds from a memory supply crunch are only getting stronger—and not just for the rest of the first half. “Beyond the June quarter, we believe memory costs will drive an increasing impact on our business,” Cook told analysts on Apple’s quarterly earnings call Thursday, according to a transcript supplied by AlphaSense.1
That could hit profits: The company forecast gross margins would come in between 47.5% and 48.5% in the June quarter, down sequentially from more than 49%.
Booming demand from AI data centers has caused the price of memory devices to skyrocket over the past year. That inflation is expected to eventually show up in the price of consumer electronics.
Apple on Thursday reported better-than-expected results on the top and bottom lines, but noted the memory shortage was already pressuring profits. Gross margins on its products declined by two percentage points to 38.7%, “driven by a seasonal loss of leverage and higher memory costs,” said CFO Kevan Parekh. Company-wide margins expanded last quarter, but only because of its services business, where margins exceeded 76%.
Memory has been one of the hottest commodities in Silicon Valley, and on Wall Street, for the past year due to a supply crunch driven by demand from AI data centers. The hyperscalers—Alphabet (GOOG), Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon (AMZN), Meta (META), and Oracle (ORCL)—are expected to spend more than $700 billion on infrastructure this year. Those deep-pocketed tech giants are paying handsome premiums to secure memory, driving up prices.
Flash memory supplier Sandisk (SNDK) on Thursday reported quarterly revenue of $5.95 billion, a 251% increase from the prior year and well over $1 billion more than it forecast early in the quarter. Data center revenue grew 233% from the prior quarter, while gross margins expanded to more than 78% from 51%.2
The shortage has made memory stocks some of the market's top performers. Micron (MU) stock is up more than 85% since the start of the year. Western Digital (WDC) and Seagate Technology (STX) have seen their share prices double this year, while Sandisk's has quadrupled.
The data center boom has generated so much demand for memory that it’s rewiring the industry. Sandisk CEO David Goeckler on Thursday said the company has signed multi-year partnerships with five customers needing to secure a consistent supply of memory. “We believe this marks a fundamental evolution of our business,” Goeckler said.3
Cook on Thursday said Apple would “look at a range of options” when considering how to adapt to soaring memory prices. It could strike multi-year contracts with memory suppliers, including Sandisk, Micron, and Samsung. Goeckler on Thursday said Sandisk was in talks with some “edge customers,” which includes PC and smartphone makers, about such deals.
Ultimately, it may be consumers who pay the price. “We expect Apple to raise the [average sales price] of new higher end iPhones (Foldable, ProMax and Pro) introduced this fall,” wrote Bank of America analysts in a note on Friday. “We see the iPhone as a relatively price inelastic product, where a $100 price increase would not materially shift the demand curve but would absorb most of the memory related margin pressure.”4
Wall Street's confidence that Apple can defray higher memory costs helped buoy shares on Friday. The stock rose 3.3% to close at a year-to-date high.
Update—May 1, 2026: This story was updated to reflect the market close on Friday.

title: Why the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Hit Record Highs While the Dow Fell Today
content:
Same market, different outcomes. Here's why Apple sent two indexes to record highs while the Dow slipped.
It's a tale of two markets on Friday, and Apple is writing most of the script. The Nasdaq-100 and S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.29%) were both sitting at fresh record highs around 10:30 a.m. ET, when things got a little wobbly.
As of this writing at 12:56 p.m. ET, the Nasdaq-100 was up 0.9%, the S&P 500 had gained 0.5%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI 0.31%) had slipped 0.1% lower.
^NDX data by YCharts
The divergence between the leading indexes reflects the outsized influence of a single stock: Apple (AAPL +3.26%).

The iPhone maker's 4.5% gain following a strong earnings report is lifting the tech-heavy Nasdaq, where it commands a 10% weighting, and the S&P 500, where it holds a 6% weighting. The Dow, which weights its 30 components by share price rather than market capitalization, is feeling more pain from Amgen's (AMGN 4.75%) earnings-based 5.7% decline. This index also took a harder hit from unexpected tariff news.

Apple absolutely crushed its earnings report Thursday evening. Exiting CEO Tim Cook said demand for the iPhone 17 and Mac computers remains strong. Apple is now flirting with its first record close since December 2025.

Amgen also beat estimates Thursday, but the strong results were overshadowed by modest guidance targets. As a high-priced stock in the price-weighted Dow, Amgen's decline is putting significant downward pressure on that index.
The late-morning pullback across all three indexes coincided with news that the Trump administration is imposing a 25% tariff on European automobiles. And oil prices dropped, with the price-tracking USO (USO 2.92%) fund falling 3.3%, after Iran sent a new peace proposal to mediators. Less drama in the Strait of Hormuz is generally good news for energy costs, though the positive developments tend to look fragile.
The Nasdaq and S&P 500 are hitting records because Apple is doing the heavy lifting. The Dow is slipping because its quirky price-weighting math gives outsized influence to a struggling biotech stock. Same market, different stories.
April was the best month for stocks since the pandemic rebound, and May is off to a good start with major indexes near all-time highs.
For long-term investors, today's divergence is a good reminder not to get too caught up in which index does what on any given afternoon. Apple's raised guidance and strong iPhone demand are real. That matters a lot more than whether the Dow closes up or down a tenth of a percent. After all, Apple's business is a pretty reliable barometer for the American consumer market's long-term resilience.
